title: Pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements

sources.locator: CSS Snapshot 2024; W3C Working Group Note 2024; provisions applicable to Pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements
sources.claim: Pseudo-classes select state or structure such as :focus-visible, :checked, :disabled, and :nth-child, while pseudo-elements represent generated boxes.

sources.locator: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2; W3C Recommendation 2023; provisions applicable to Pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements
sources.claim: Pseudo-classes select state or structure such as :focus-visible, :checked, :disabled, and :nth-child, while pseudo-elements represent generated boxes.

canonicalExplanation.summary: **Pseudo-classes** match elements in a **state**: `:hover` (pointer over it), `:focus-visible` (keyboard focus that should be shown), `:checked`, `:disabled`, `:invalid`, `:user-invalid`, and structural ones like `:first-child` and `:nth-child(odd)`. **Pseudo-elements** style a **part** or generated box: `::before`, `::after`, `::placeholder`, `::marker`. Hover-only styling leaves keyboard and touch users out — always give `:focus-visible` its own clear style.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
Your buttons light up beautifully on hover. A keyboard user tabs through the page and sees… nothing change at all, because an old reset removed outlines. On a phone, there's no hover either. A control has visible :focus-visible styling independent of its hover styling. In this lesson you'll implement hover, focus-visible, validation and structural states without hiding keyboard focus.

```predict
{"question": "A menu opens only on `:hover`. Can a keyboard user open it?", "options": ["Yes", "No — keyboard focus doesn't trigger :hover"], "answer": 1, "why": "Hover requires a pointer. Keyboard and many touch users never trigger it. Use :focus-within, a button toggle, or both."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Specificity and source order**, **Text and page semantics**, **Type, class, attribute and combinator selectors**, and **Labels and input controls** — many states belong to form controls.

sections.heading: The model: states and parts
sections.body:
```css
.btn:hover { background: #1d4ed8; }
.btn:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #f59e0b; outline-offset: 2px; }  /* keyboard */
.btn:disabled { opacity: 0.6; cursor: not-allowed; }

input:user-invalid { border-color: #b91c1c; }   /* only after the user interacts */
tr:nth-child(even) { background: #f3f4f6; }       /* zebra stripes */
.required::after { content: " *"; }             /* generated, decorative */
```

| Selector | Matches |
|---|---|
| `:hover`. | pointer over the element. |
| `:focus-visible`. | focused and the browser judges focus should be shown (e.g. keyboard). |
| `:user-invalid`. | invalid after the user has interacted. |
| `:nth-child(even)`. | every second child. |
| `::after`. | a generated box after the content. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why `:focus-visible` instead of `:focus`?", "answer": "`:focus` also fires on mouse clicks, which some designers dislike, so they remove it — hurting keyboard users. `:focus-visible` shows focus when it's needed, so there's no reason to hide it."}
```

sections.heading: Never hide focus

includes: Style hover, focus-visible, disabled, validation and structural states.
Use pseudo-elements for decorative parts and keep focus always visible.

outcomes: Implement hover, focus-visible, validation and structural states without hiding keyboard focus.

examples.title: Focus that doesn't depend on hover
examples.situation: A control has visible :focus-visible styling independent of its hover styling.
walkthrough: **Hover:** `.btn:hover` darkens the background for pointer users.
**Independent :focus-visible:** `.btn:focus-visible` adds a 3px amber outline with offset — a different, clearly visible style.
**Test:** Tab to the button; the browser will render the outline even with no mouse present.
examples.result: Keyboard users can always see which control has focus, whether or not anyone hovers.

examples.title: The error shown too early
examples.situation: A sign-up form uses `input:invalid { border: red }`. Every empty required field is red before the user types anything.
walkthrough: Users feel scolded before they start.
Fix: `input:user-invalid` so the red border (plus a text message) appears only after the user has interacted.
examples.result: Errors appear after users interact, not the moment the page loads.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: If an interface works on :hover, it automatically works for keyboard and touch users.
misconceptions.correction: Hover depends on a pointer; keyboard and many touch users never trigger it. Provide :focus-visible styles and keyboard-reachable controls, and never make essential content hover-only.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why couldn't the keyboard user open the menu?

analogy.example: Pseudo-classes are like **status lights on a machine**: "power on" (hover), "selected" (focus), "out of order" (disabled). If one light only works when someone touches the machine with a mouse, people using the keypad never see it.
usefulFor: remembering each state needs its own visible signal
limitations: Machines have fixed lights; CSS states can be styled any way.
Pseudo-elements are like stickers added to the machine — decoration, not new parts.

steps.explanation: Hover styling applies only when a pointer is over the button.
The control has visible :focus-visible styling independent of its hover styling.
Keyboard users still see where focus is.

trace.textAlternative: Independent hover and focus styles. Step 1, Hover style: pointer is over; background is #1d4ed8. Hover styling applies only when a pointer is over the button. Step 2, Keyboard focus: focus-visible is true; outline is 3px amber. The control has visible :focus-visible styling independent of its hover styling. Step 3, No pointer: hover is false; focus visible is yes. Keyboard users still see where focus is.

remediation.explanation: For every interactive element, list its states — **default, hover, focus-visible, active, disabled, invalid** — and check each has a visible style. Use DevTools' ":hov" panel to force them.

recap.summary: To implement hover, focus-visible, validation and structural states, give every state its own visible style, prefer :focus-visible and :user-invalid, use pseudo-elements for decorative parts, and never hide keyboard focus.
